analysis.one_liner: Bars large pension plans from cutting future benefit accruals for long-serving older workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate vote; it was referred to the Finance Committee in June 1999 and died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped employers with defined benefit pension plans covering 100 or more workers from adopting plan changes that reduce the benefits workers earn for future years of service. Under the rules before this bill, a plan could freeze or shrink the yearly benefit growth for existing workers while protecting only benefits already earned. The bill would have protected the whole expected benefit—including early retirement subsidies—for workers at large plans for amendments adopted after June 29, 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Older and long-serving employees at large companies with traditional defined benefit pensions, who would keep the benefit accrual rates they had when hired rather than seeing them reduced mid-career. Workers near early-retirement eligibility would also keep retirement subsidies they were counting on.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in large traditional pension plans

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits plan amendments in large defined benefit plans (100 or more participants) that reduce future accrued benefits for years of service [S2][S3].
Counts early retirement benefits and retirement-type subsidies as protected accrued benefits for workers who meet the plan's conditions [S3].
Applies to plan amendments adopted after June 29, 1999, protecting current workers from mid-career benefit cuts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sponsors of large defined benefit pension plans—mostly large employers—would lose the flexibility to reduce future accruals for existing employees, a tool often used to trim long-term pension costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers with defined benefit pensions

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers plans with 100 or more participants, so workers at smaller plans would remain exposed to wearing-away amendments [S3].

Employers and plan sponsors commonly argue that locking in benefit accrual formulas reduces their ability to modernize pension plans (for example, moving to portable designs), and can raise the cost of maintaining traditional pensions—pressures that can lead employers to freeze or close plans altogether. This trade-off is not addressed in the bill text or the summary [S3][S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers at large traditional pension plans, the protection is meaningful: it stops mid-career cuts to the benefits they are counting on for retirement. The cost falls on employers, who would lose a cost-cutting lever; the legitimate concern is that locking in old formulas may hasten the decline of traditional pensions, but the bill does nothing to address that risk and offers no help to workers at smaller plans.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in June 1999, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the Older Workers Pension Protection Act of 1999 on June 29, 1999 [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action—no hearing, markup, or floor vote—appears in the action history, and the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sponsors of large defined benefit pension plans, who kept the ability to reduce future benefit accruals for long-serving workers under existing law.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never took action on the bill; it died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, but no votes or statements of opposition appear in the record—the bill simply never moved after referral [S1][S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large employers sponsoring defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: The bill would have required them to keep paying benefit accruals at existing rates for current workers, closing off a common way to reduce long-term pension obligations. Existing law allowed these 'wearing away' amendments, which shift pension cost risk onto older workers.
New anti-cut rules would have complicated plan administration for large plans, but the bill never advanced so the practical effect was nil.
